findings.title: Local cache is populated before the limited insert, so a rejected device is admitted on its next request
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache entry remains for ~29 minutes. On the device's very next request `localCache.Get(key)` hits, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, `TagDevice` returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` issues an identity. The new device limit therefore only rejects the first request from an over-limit device; a reload (which the browser/UI will naturally do) bypasses the limit entirely, and the device is never written to the DB so it isn't even counted. The cache must be set only after a successful write (or removed on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`).

findings.title: Device limit is trivially bypassed by clients that omit the X-Grafana-Device-Id header or have an unparsable address
findings.body: `TagDevice` returns nil (no error) when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is absent and also when `network.GetIPFromAddress` fails. Since `Anonymous.Authenticate` only denies access on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, any anonymous client that simply does not send the device header (curl, scripts, API consumers, a browser with the header stripped) is authenticated regardless of the configured `device_limit`. If the limit is intended as an enforcement mechanism rather than best-effort UI accounting, requests without a device ID should be rejected when a limit is configured, or the limitation should be clearly documented.

findings.title: Count-then-insert is not atomic; concurrent new devices can exceed the configured limit
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` in one session and the INSERT/upsert in a separate `WithDbSession` call, with no transaction or lock. N concurrent first-time anonymous requests arriving while `count == deviceLimit-1` will all observe a count below the limit and all insert, so the stored device count can exceed `deviceLimit` by the degree of concurrency. Enforcing the limit in a single transaction (or with a serverlock/advisory lock) is required for the limit to be a hard cap.

findings.title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine into the synchronous auth path, adding a COUNT(*) plus write to request latency
findings.body: Previously tagging ran in a detached goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout; now `TagDevice` executes inline inside `Authenticate` using the request context. For every uncached device this adds a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ...` (full range scan on a table that can hold tens of thousands of rows when a limit is configured) plus an INSERT/UPDATE before the identity is returned, and any DB slowness now directly delays or fails anonymous page loads. The local cache mitigates this per device for ~29 minutes but not for first requests or multi-instance deployments. Consider caching the count or using a cheaper check, and only blocking on the DB when a limit is configured.

findings.title: Limit test does not cover the update path for an existing device or the cache bypass
findings.body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a second, new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. It does not verify that an already-registered device can still be updated when the limit is reached (the `updateDevice` branch returning nil), that a device whose last update is older than 30 days is rejected, or that the service layer (`TagDevice`/`Authenticate`) actually denies the device on repeated requests. The last case would have caught the local-cache bypass in `tagDeviceUI`.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit is typed as `undefined` and never actually undefined at runtime
findings.body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` makes TypeScript infer the property type as the literal `undefined` (under strictNullChecks), so consumers of `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` cannot use it as a number without a cast. Meanwhile the backend DTO field is a plain `int64` without `omitempty`, so the JSON always contains a number (0 when unset) and the `number | undefined` declaration in `GrafanaConfig` is misleading. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit = 0` / `number` and treat 0 as 'no limit', or make the backend field a pointer with `omitempty`.

findings.title: New `device_limit` setting is not added to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini or the configuration docs
findings.body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, but the PR adds no entry to `conf/defaults.ini`/`conf/sample.ini` and no documentation for the setting or its semantics (0 = unlimited, 30-day window, what users see when rejected). Administrators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists, and Grafana's convention is that every ini key has a documented default.

findings.title: ProvideAnonDBStore signature change may break wire generation if the store is still listed as a provider
findings.body: `ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an `int64` argument and `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now takes `db.DB` instead of `anonstore.AnonStore`. The previous signature implies the store was being provided via dependency injection (wire); `pkg/server/wire.go` is not in this change set. If `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` is still registered in the wire set, `wire gen` will fail with no provider for `int64`; if it is not removed and was bound to `anonstore.AnonStore`, the binding becomes dead. Please verify the wire set was updated.
